title: Three Shrines at Hanamakonda
subtitle: When Stone Learned to Share the Gods
era: Thousand Pillar Temple and Kakatiya craft, c. 1163-1175 CE
moral: Shared spaces can turn difference into harmony.

sources.note: Sovereignty context for Rudradeva's Hanamakonda building age.

sources.citation: ASI documentation for Thousand Pillar Temple, Hanamakonda, Monument of National Importance
sources.note: Site record for the trikutalayam plan, pillars, Nandi and restoration history.

sources.citation: UNESCO Tentative List submission for Warangal Fort, Kakatiya Kala Thoranam and Thousand Pillar Temple, India, 2010
sources.note: Recent heritage framing of Kakatiya architectural serial sites.

panels.shot: sweeping low-angle wide of temple complex under dawn sky

dialogue.text: In Hanamakonda, between war and water, Rudradeva and his stone guilds dared a temple where Shiva, Vishnu and Surya shared one shining floor.

panels.shot: slow push-in on inscription being carved

dialogue.text: In 1163, an inscription at Anumakonda named Rudradeva as ruler, fixing his sovereignty in stone while his mind turned to what new stone could yet do.

panels.shot: wide documentary shot of Hanamakonda landscape with fort walls

dialogue.text: Around Hanamakonda, tanks, embankments and fort walls grew. For the Kakatiyas, stone was not only for gods, but for water, defense and rule.

panels.shot: architectural top-down sketch shot over plans

dialogue.text: From these stone-workers came a question: could one platform carry three shrines, three traditions, without fracture?

panels.shot: medium shot circling around Rudradeva in council

dialogue.speaker: rudradeva_and_kakatiya_stone_guilds
dialogue.text: If my land has many paths to the divine, why must stone walk only one?

panels.shot: dynamic low-angle of craftsmen at quarry

dialogue.text: Guilds mobilised. Quarries answered with great blocks. The planned trikutalayam needed stone that could bear both weight and meaning.

panels.shot: architectural overhead of star-shaped foundation layout

dialogue.text: Instead of a plain square, they traced a star. The platform itself would shift and turn, catching light differently at every hour.
Their pillars were not lowly supports. They polished them until stone caught and returned a man’s face, as if the temple itself watched.

panels.shot: wide interior view of rising mandapa forest of columns

dialogue.text: Later ages called it the Thousand Pillar Temple. The record shows many pillars, varied and deliberate, each speaking a different rhythm of craft.

panels.shot: medium shot of sculptors planning monolithic Nandi

dialogue.text: From one stone, they planned Nandi, Shiva’s bull. Not assembled, but carved whole, a single mass made patient, powerful and alert.

panels.shot: dramatic side view of Nandi partially carved

dialogue.speaker: rudradeva_and_kakatiya_stone_guilds
dialogue.text: When Nandi looks, let him look over all three shrines, not one alone.

panels.shot: sunlit wide shot of completed triple sanctums

dialogue.text: By the mid-1170s, the trikutalayam stood. Shiva, Vishnu and the Sun, three garbhagrihas sharing one carefully turned base.

panels.shot: intimate interior shot showing different worshippers

dialogue.text: In the cool hall, Shaiva, Vaishnava and Saura rites unfolded side by side. Shared pillars held prayers that did not sound the same.

panels.shot: low-angle shot of Rudradeva walking through mandapa

dialogue.text: For Rudradeva, this mandapa was more than piety. It displayed a kingdom where different devotions could stand under one carved roof.

panels.shot: time-lapse style wide shot hinting at centuries passing

dialogue.text: Centuries tested the stone. Weather, change of rulers, and neglect left scars, but the triple-shrine idea remained visible in the ground plan.

panels.shot: modern documentary shot of ASI conservators at work

dialogue.text: Modern conservation teams returned, guided by records and fragments, to stabilise the mandapa and recover as much of the Kakatiya design as time allowed.

panels.shot: wide shot linking Thousand Pillar Temple with Warangal Fort and Kala Thoranam

dialogue.text: In UNESCO’s tentative list, Hanamakonda’s shrine sits with Warangal’s fort and Kala Thoranam, part of a serial story of Kakatiya stone, power and imagination.

panels.shot: quiet close-up of Nandi facing the triple shrines at dusk

dialogue.text: Hanamakonda’s three shrines remind us that difference need not mean distance: with care, one platform, one hall, one city can let many ways of worship stand together.
